The Lower Saxony data protection authority fined notebooksbilliger.de AG EUR 10.4 million for video surveillance of its employees over at least two years without a legal basis. Cameras covered workplaces, sales rooms, warehouses and break areas, and some also covered customer seating areas. Recordings were often kept for 60 days, longer than necessary. The company has since made its video surveillance lawful. The fine was not yet final at the time of the press release.

A window-fitting-hardware manufacturer sent a customer a letter in January 2020 about possibly faulty fittings, having obtained her name and address from the window seller. The complainant said the company had processed her data for about five months without informing her and that the letter did not meet Article 14 GDPR. The Austrian DSB held that the company breached its information duty by not stating the legal basis for processing, and ordered it to provide that information within four weeks. The other complaints (timing, other Article 14 content, and language) were dismissed, as the information was given during the proceedings and the German-language procedure was considered sufficient.

A public medical university posted recordings of practical paediatric exams on an e-learning platform, which showed students presenting student cards and ID cards. The university did not report the breach to the President of UODO or notify the affected students, judging the risk low. The President found a high risk, held that Art. 33(1) and Art. 34(1) GDPR were breached, ordered the students to be notified within 3 days of the decision becoming final, and imposed a fine of PLN 25,000.

A former employee of a medical business copied the personal data of 100 patients to market his own services, and the business notified the breach to UODO but chose not to inform the patients despite rating the risk as high. UODO ordered it in February 2020 to notify the patients with the content required by Article 34(2). The business sent incomplete notices and failed to prove it had complied, and ignored guidance from UODO staff. UODO therefore fined it PLN 85,588 (the equivalent of EUR 20,000) under Article 83(6) for not complying with a corrective order.

The Polish DPA imposed a fine of €5000 on a company for failing to comply with the obligation to cooperate with the supervisory authority and not providing it with all information necessary to fulfil its tasks in the course of the proceedings.

The report describes a case in which a Hessian police officer, over a long period and with no official reason, searched several people from his family circle in various police systems. The Hessian data protection commissioner issued fines for these violations totalling EUR 1,800. The fine notice has since become final. Before that, the public prosecutor had closed its criminal investigation into breach of private secrets because it could not be shown that the data were passed on to third parties. The case is one of several examples of 'employee excess' (Mitarbeiterexzess) by police staff.

In its 2021 annual report the Hessian data protection authority describes a case of employee excess: a police officer repeatedly looked up a colleague in the police information systems ComVor and POLAS with no official reason, out of private curiosity about rumours of criminal proceedings. The authority imposed an administrative fine of EUR 500 on the officer. No appeal was lodged against the fine decision. The report gives no articles for this specific case.

After separating from his partner, a Hessian police officer used the official residents' register system (EWO), which he had access to for work, to look up his ex-partner's new address. He then travelled to her new home and met her at the entrance, and she reported this to the police. The Hessian data protection commissioner treated this as an employee excess (private use of official data) and fined the officer EUR 600 in total. The fine notice is final. The annual report describes the case only briefly and does not state the articles for this case.

In the annual report for 2021 the Hessian data protection commissioner describes a case of 'employee excess'. A police chief inspector bought a laptop privately on an online platform. When the seller would not renegotiate the payment method, he used the police information system POLAS to look up the seller. He then sent the seller messages quoting the seller's date and place of birth and current and former addresses, to press his demand. The seller reported the matter, and the authority fined the officer EUR 400. The report names no articles for this individual case.

A guest at a bistro complained about cold food and left without paying. To track the guest down, bistro staff phoned several visitors using the numbers those visitors had left for Corona contact tracing. The Hessian authority found that this breached the purpose limitation principle of Art. 5(1)(b) GDPR. It fined the bistro's owner EUR 170. The fine was set low because of the owner's pandemic-hit finances, his insight into the wrongdoing and his constructive cooperation. The report presents the case anonymously as an example of 'employee excess' in the use of contact-tracing lists.

The Berlin DPA's 2021 annual report describes a fine against a specialist clinic that used 21 cameras inside its premises to film patients and staff around the clock, to protect against crime and property damage. The clinic argued that staff consent in their employment contracts covered this, but the consent failed for lack of voluntariness given the pressure of the employment relationship. Visible signs did not amount to valid consent from patients entering the monitored rooms, and the clinic gave no justification for the surveillance. The report gives no fine amount and does not name the articles infringed.

The Berlin data protection authority's 2021 annual report says it imposed a fine on a beverage trading company that filmed the public street next to its business premises with video cameras. The report does not give the amount of this fine, the articles breached or the date of the decision. For the year as a whole the authority says it imposed fines in 61 cases, totalling EUR 133,350; that figure covers all its fines of 2021, not this one.

The Berlin authority fined a lawyer who, for two years, published on his blog the full name and home addresses of a former client and of the client's family members, plus unredacted case-file documents, to pressure payment of a disputed debt. He claimed press privilege, but the authority found the publication was not journalistic and that his interests did not justify the processing. He removed the post after the fine proceedings began and cooperated, which reduced the fine. The report gives no amount for this fine.

The 2021 annual report of the Berlin data protection authority describes a fine against a specialist clinic. The clinic had appointed its clinic head, who was also a shareholder, as its data protection officer. The report explains that a company must ensure that the officer's other tasks do not lead to a conflict of interest, and that the management cannot appoint itself as officer. The report gives no amount for this fine and does not name the clinic.

A real estate agent wrote a letter to a citizen offering to sell the plot of land he owned. He had not given her his data, was surprised how she knew he owned it and where he lived, and asked her where she had the information from. She only replied that she could not say for reasons of data protection. When the authority took up the matter, she relied on a right to refuse information and said the data had already been deleted. When she wrote to him again, his data were still stored in a separate Christmas-greeting folder of her IT system; she admitted she had overlooked it when deleting. The authority found that she had no legal basis for direct marketing and that her answer to him did not meet the requirements of Article 12(4) GDPR. It imposed one fine for both breaches, described only as four-figure.

The Brandenburg data protection authority's 2021 activity report describes a fine imposed on a child and adolescent psychotherapist who created a WhatsApp group of about 230 people to announce her new practice address. Group members could see each other's phone numbers, and some could infer that children they knew were patients, without consent or another legal basis. The complaint came from the mother of a former minor patient. The authority fined the doctor for unlawful processing under Article 6, but the report gives only a 'four-figure' amount and no exact figure.

The Hamburg data protection authority fined a company based in Hamburg that works in health care for inadequate technical and organisational measures (Art. 32(1) GDPR). Doctors' letters with patient data were repeatedly sent to a doctor of the same name who was not the patients' treating doctor. The recipient had pointed out the mistake several times and the company had put a block (Sperrvermerk) on her in its system, but it had not made sure that the block was kept in software updates, so after an update she received letters again. The company also could not show which employees had read patient data, although there were concrete signs of an unauthorised read access. The authority imposed a fine in the low six-digit range, which the company accepted without objection.

A private individual secretly filmed young, lightly dressed women and girls in Hamburg streets and shopping centres, some apparently under 14. Police seized 156 video files made between 2013 and 2020. The case came to the HmbBfDI from the public prosecutor. The authority found there was no consent or legal basis for the processing and that the household exemption did not apply. It fined the person EUR 5,000 for the 13 cases, which the HmbBfDI calls the highest fine it has imposed on a private person since the GDPR began to apply. The person accepted the fine and did not appeal.

The Lower Saxony data protection commissioner's 2021 annual report describes a case against an electronics store. Its video surveillance cameras, which recorded image and sound, were accessible without protection, and their live images appeared on a public website. After a tip-off the authority opened an inspection. It found that the sound recording was not necessary, that the monitoring of staff had no legal basis, that the images were kept longer than needed, that a data protection impact assessment should have been done, and a clear breach of the principle of integrity and confidentiality. The store was not relieved by the fact that the website operator had acted unlawfully. Because of these several infringements, each committed at least negligently, the authority opened administrative fine proceedings. After a discussion aimed at an agreed fine range, it imposed EUR 16,000, at the low end of that range. The store objected to the fine notice; the objection had not been finally decided by the end of the reporting period.

The Saxon Data Protection Commissioner's 2021 annual report describes four administrative fines imposed on private individuals in the non-public sector. One case concerned the former owner of a fitness studio who, in a public Facebook apology for a late opening, blamed a named employee and exposed further personal data about him to club members. The authority treated this as an administrative offence. The report gives a combined amount of EUR 1,300 for the four fines and no separate amount for this case.

A bank employee repeatedly looked at a customer's account data over about a year without any business reason, because of a private connection to that customer. The customer learned of it through a request for access to his data held by the bank. The authority found no legal basis for the access and held the employee personally responsible, not the bank. It imposed a fine on the employee; the report gives no amount.

The report describes a fine against a restaurant operator in Saarland. About 120 guest contact-registration forms, collected because of COVID-19 rules, were found left in an open container after a municipal operations team reported them. The authority's investigation also found that the forms were kept in a room accessible to all staff without any security measures. The authority held that the operator had not taken effective technical and organisational measures under Art. 32, with Art. 5(1)(f) and Art. 24, and imposed a fine under Art. 83(1) and (5)(a). The text gives no amount.

The annual report of the Saarland data protection authority for 2021 describes, in section 5.3, a fine proceeding over an email sent with an open distribution list by an employee of a members' office. The addressees' names and email addresses were visible, and the content revealed their political views. The authority held the office, as the controller, responsible for its employee's conduct and issued the fine notice against the office under Art. 83(5)(a) GDPR. The report gives no amount for this fine.

The Slovak Data Protection Office's 2021 annual report says that the highest fine it imposed that year was EUR 40,000 on a controller (not named in the report). The fine was for breaching the accountability principle (no data protection impact assessment proven), the fairness and transparency principle, and Article 28 (no processor contract in place). The report says the fine was legally binding.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a warning to the Town Hall of Tobar for publicly posting a list with the personal data of citizens on jury duty on a street. The DPA considered this a breach of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

The Romanian DPA completed an investigation at ING Bank N.V. Amsterdam – Bucharest Branch on 7 December 2020. It found that the bank kept processing a former customer's personal data and sent update-request emails after the customer had asked to close their last account in 2017. A system error left the business relationship marked as active. The bank was fined RON 14,619.9 (about EUR 3,000) for breaching the Article 5(1)(a)-(d) principles and Article 6(1) lawfulness.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) sanctioned Vodafone España, S.A.U. for non-compliance with general data processing principles. The initial proposed fine was €90,000 however, it was reduced to €54,000 for recognition of responsibility and making an early payment of the fine.

The Romanian supervisory authority investigated Qualitance QBS SA after several complaints. The company had sent one email to 295 job candidates with all recipients' email addresses visible to each other. The authority found the company had not implemented sufficient security measures, breaching Article 32 GDPR. A fine of 4,867.50 lei (stated as equivalent to EUR 1,000) was imposed, along with a corrective measure requiring compliant technical and organisational measures for remote transmission of personal data, including regular staff training.

A complaint was lodged about the Belgian FPS Finance requiring citizens to log in with a Microsoft user account to download a VAT brochure from its FisconetPlus website. The Litigation Chamber examined the access options, cookie consent practices and related data protection duties. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 6(1), 7, 25(1) and 35 GDPR. It issued a reprimand and imposed no fine, because it has no power to fine public bodies, and it ordered no compliance measures because the Microsoft login option had been removed from the site.

A complainant filed a complaint against a street-parking company (first respondent) and a bailiff's office collecting its debts (second respondent). The Litigation Chamber found breaches of transparency/information duties, access rights, lawful basis, data minimisation and accountability. It reprimanded both respondents, issued compliance orders, and fined the parking company EUR 50,000 and the bailiff's office EUR 15,000. A note at the top says the Market Court annulled the whole decision on 26 May 2021, though later case law again allowed fines for a first infringement.

A complainant filed a complaint against a street-parking company and the bailiff's office that collected its debts. The Litigation Chamber found both breached transparency and information duties, lawfulness, data minimisation and accountability rules. It reprimanded both and ordered each to bring its practices into compliance. It fined the parking company EUR 50,000 and the bailiff's office EUR 15,000. The Market Court later annulled the whole decision, mainly because of the fine.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) initiated a sanctioning procedure against the utility company, Iberdrola Clientes, S.A.U for infringing Article 21 GDPR, Article 48(1)(b) LGT, and Article 23(4) LOPDGDD. The initial proposed fine was €10000 however, it was reduced to €6000, for recognition of responsibility and early payment of the fine.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €60000 (reduced to €36000) on Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria, SA. (BBVA) for processing personal data without the accuracy required according to Article 5(1)(d) GDPR.

An natural person received a warning from the Spanish DPA (AEPD) for tweeting a photo of a bill where the name, surname, fiscal ID and bank account of a restaurant owner was visible. This constituted a breach of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.

The respondent sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of natural persons from 2 November to 3 December 2020, reaching 376 persons, during the state of emergency when sending data messages was free. It had no legal basis for processing and did not give the information required by Article 14. The Czech authority found two offences by penalty order and imposed one fine of CZK 208,000 for the more serious offence (Article 6(1)), applying the absorption principle.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that, from 2 November to 3 December 2020, sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of 1,743 natural persons without any legal basis and without giving the Article 14 information. It found breaches of Article 6(1) and Article 14 GDPR. Applying the absorption principle, it imposed a single fine of CZK 235,000, based on the more serious unlawful-processing offence. Aggravating factors were the abuse of free data boxes during the state of emergency, the large number of people affected and the breach of several obligations.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a legal person that sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of 2,566 natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020. It had no legal basis for processing and did not give the Article 14 information. The authority found two offences and, applying the absorption principle, imposed a single fine of CZK 251,000. Aggravating factors included the abuse of free data box messaging during the state of emergency and the large number of people affected.

The Czech DPA issued a penal order against a company that sent unsolicited marketing offers to natural persons through their data boxes (datové schránky) between 2 November and 3 December 2020, without any legal basis. The company also did not give the Article 14 information to those data subjects. The DPA found two administrative offences (Art. 6(1) and Art. 14) and imposed a fine of 295,000 CZK. The text is an order that can be challenged by objection (rozklad) within 15 days.

The Czech DPA issued a penal order (příkaz) against a company that sent unsolicited offers to natural persons through their data boxes between 2 November and 3 December 2020. The company had no legal basis for this processing and did not give the required Article 14 information to the data subjects. It was found liable for an infringement of Article 6(1) and one of Article 14 GDPR, and fined CZK 205,000 under the absorption principle, near the lowest statutory level.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that sent unsolicited commercial offers through the data boxes of natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020. It had no legal basis for processing and did not provide the Article 14 information. The Ministry of the Interior reported that 6,119 natural persons were contacted. The company was fined CZK 322,000 under the absorption principle, with the unlawful processing treated as the most serious offence.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a controller that, from 2 November to 3 December 2020, sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of individuals, contacting 4,238 natural persons. It had no legal basis for this under Article 6(1) and did not give the Article 14 information. The two offences were handled together and a single fine of CZK 285,000 was imposed. The authority treated the conduct as especially harmful because it took place during the state of emergency, when sending data messages was free.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against an association that, between 2 November and 3 December 2020, sent unsolicited offers to 23,302 natural persons through their official data boxes. It had no legal basis for processing their data and gave them none of the Article 14 information. The Office found two offences, applied the absorption principle, and imposed a single fine of CZK 666,000. The order can be challenged by an objection within 8 days.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a legal person that sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020, reaching 1,035 individuals. It had no legal basis for processing and did not give the information required by Article 14. The two offences were handled together and a single fine of CZK 221,000 was imposed under the absorption principle, based on the more serious unlawful-processing offence. The conduct was treated as aggravated because it took place during the state of emergency, when data box messages were free, and involved a large number of people.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that, from 2 November to 3 December 2020, sent unsolicited offers to individuals' official data boxes without any legal basis. It contacted 1,060 natural persons and did not give them the Article 14 information. The authority found breaches of Article 6(1) and Article 14 GDPR and, applying the absorption principle, imposed one fine of CZK 221,000 under Article 83(5). The fine was aggravated by the abuse of free data box messaging during the state of emergency, the large number of people affected and the multiple breaches.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020. According to the Ministry of the Interior, it contacted 80 natural persons this way. The Office found that it had no legal basis for processing (Art. 6(1)) and did not give the information required by Art. 14. It imposed a single fine of CZK 202,000, applying the absorption principle, based on the more serious offence (unlawful processing).

A charitable company sent a person a further postal request for a donation on 13 November 2020, although he had asked in November 2018 for his personal data to be erased and objected to direct marketing. The Czech DPA, acting through a penalty order, found the company guilty of an offence for breaching the right to erasure under Article 17(1)(c) GDPR. It imposed a fine of CZK 5,000. The company may file an objection within 8 days, which would cancel the order and continue the proceedings.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued an advisory opinion about the use of personal data for advertising purposes on Facebook and joint controllership. It underlined that each controller needs a legal basis for processing personal data.

The Polish DPA issued a warning to a sole proprietor for the lack of cooperation with the supervisory authority in the performance of its tasks and the failure to provide information necessary for the DPA perform its tasks.

A complainant, who wanted to stay anonymous, complained that a car wash used CCTV without signage or privacy-policy disclosure, and that images with customers' number plates and staff were posted on the operator's Facebook page. The Litigation Chamber found that the complainant had only a public interest and no personal interest or standing, and that the procedure had been tainted by a procedural defect because the complaint should have been dismissed once anonymity was requested. It therefore dismissed the complaint without ruling on the merits. No fine or order was imposed.

The Swedish DPA (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten) audited Swedish Customs' personal data breaches routines. No serious violations were found, however the DPA gave several recommendations as per the Swedish Criminal Data Act (the "GDPR" for Swedish law enforcement agencies).

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation on 26 November 2020 into Banca Transilvania SA after complaints. A statement a client had given the bank about how he intended to use a sum of money was circulated among employees by email, printed, photographed and shared on WhatsApp, then posted on Facebook and a website. This exposed personal data of four people (one client, three employees). The authority found breaches of Articles 32(1) and (2) with 5(1)(f) GDPR, including insufficient measures and ineffective staff training, and fined the bank RON 487,380 (about EUR 100,000).

The French DPA (CNIL) imposed a €6,000 fine on a private doctor for violating Article 32 GDPR by making his patients' health data freely accessible on the web, and Article 33 GDPR by not notifying the DPA of said breach.

The Polish DPA (UODO) imposed a fine of €250,000 (1,069,850 PLN) on a loan company for failing to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, which resulted in a breach of data confidentiality.

Rome Municipality used the 'TuPassi' appointment-booking system, supplied by Miropass, since 2015 for users and employees. An earlier Garante decision (no. 81 of 7 March 2019) found the processing unlawful and ordered corrective actions, which the municipality eventually completed. In this injunction order the Garante confirmed violations of Articles 5, 13, 14, 28 and 32 GDPR and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 500,000, with publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ceased.

The Italian DPA inspected the 'Tupassi' appointment-booking system supplied by Miropass to public bodies and private entities, including healthcare facilities. It found that health-related booking data were processed without specific consent, that the company did maintenance and support with access to clients' systems without being appointed processor, that it had not regulated its relationship with booking 'broker' agents, and that user data were kept for an indefinite time. Because the company had remedied most issues during the proceedings, no further corrective measures were imposed except an order to update the online privacy notices. A fine of EUR 40,000 was imposed and the decision is to be published.

After a report from a general practitioner about the 'proactive healthcare' (sanità di iniziativa) model, the Garante inspected the Tuscany South-East local health authority. From 2018 the authority collected named lists of enrolled chronic patients from GPs, passed through USB sticks and e-mail to the regional body ESTAR, without a DPIA, with incomplete privacy notices, an outdated processor designation and no records register at inspection time. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, found no need for further corrective measures because the conduct had ceased and the authority had remedied matters, and imposed a fine of EUR 100,000 plus publication of the decision.

The DPC opened an inquiry into seven personal data breaches notified by University College Dublin, in which third parties accessed UCD email accounts or login credentials were posted online. It found UCD failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data in its email service, kept some personal data longer than necessary, and notified one breach 13 days after becoming aware of it. The DPC imposed an administrative fine of €70,000, ordered UCD to bring its email service processing into compliance, and issued a reprimand.

The Italian DPA received a complaint that the municipality of Santo Stefano Belbo had published on its website a decision containing a person's name, details of court proceedings against the municipality, the legal costs awarded and her bank IBAN. Even after the IBAN was removed, the documents stayed online in the archive section beyond the 15-day period for the notice board, for over two years. The Garante found the IBAN excessive and the continued publication without a legal basis, in breach of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Italian Code. It fined the municipality EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the data had been removed.

A municipal councillor complained that a municipality kept a municipal executive resolution on its website, showing that the mayor had filed a criminal complaint against him, for longer than the 15 days allowed for publication. The Garante also found that the municipality had not appointed a Data Protection Officer or notified the DPO's contact details by 25 May 2018. It found breaches of the lawfulness and data minimisation principles and of Article 37, and fined the municipality EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because the data had been removed and the DPO's details communicated.

A data subject asked the Lazio regional social workers' professional body for access to his own and his two minor daughters' personal data on 27 November 2019, but received no reply. After the Garante intervened, the body answered only on 17 June 2020, and without explaining the reasons for the delay or the complaint and judicial remedies. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR, imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) ordered a resident of an apartment building to stop surveilling other residents and public spaces through CCTV cameras installed in the resident's apartment and car. The DPA concluded that the processing did not comply with the GDPR, and ordered the resident to delete the footage.

The Irish DPA found that Groupon infringed the principle of data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR) by requiring the complainant to verify their identity by submitting a copy of a national ID document when a less data-driven solution to the question of identity verification was available. The DPC also found that Groupon infringed Articles 12(2),17(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR.

After a public-interest report, the Hungarian authority inspected and then opened its own proceeding against a lender offering state-subsidised baby-expectation loans. The lender had copied complete pregnancy care books and discharge reports of applicants, including health data not needed to prove the 12th week of pregnancy. The authority found breaches of data minimisation, lack of legal basis (including for health data) and lack of clear, transparent information. It ordered deletion of the copies and reform of the information practice, and fined the lender HUF 35,000,000.
The Slovenian DPA issued an opinion on the case of an employee participation in the production of a company's video greeting card under article 6 (1) and 4 (11) of the GDPR.
The Slovenian DPA advised on whether a gym teacher's decision to ask children to record their dance videos and submit them to an online classroom was in accordance with Article 6 GDPR.
The Hungarian DPA (NAIH) found a violation of Article 15 GDPR and obliged a controller to grant a complainant access to his personal data.

Datainspektionen found that Uppsalahem AB, a landlord, breached Article 6(1)(f) GDPR by running camera surveillance from 25 February to 14 May 2020 on the first-floor common areas of a residential building. The camera also filmed residents' apartment doors and parts of their homes. The authority accepted the aim of stopping disturbances as a legitimate interest and the camera as necessary, but found that residents' privacy interest weighed more heavily. A fine of SEK 300 000 was imposed; a reprimand and orders were rejected because the surveillance had already ended.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) issued a warning against the Bucharest Municipality - District 4 as the General Directorate of 4th District Local Police breached Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR. The warning was issued along with a corrective measure.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) issued a warning to the Cluj-Napoca Municipality as the General Directorate of Local Police breached Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR. The warning was issued along with a corrective measure.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a warning sanction on a private individual for failing to comply with the right to information (Article 13 GDPR) when collecting personal data on its website.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) imposed a warning sanction against the State Tax Administration Agency (AEAT) for infringing Article 5(1)(d) GDPR, i.e. lack of accuracy in the processing of personal data.

Umeå University sent a police investigation protocol containing health, sexual-life and criminal-suspicion data by unencrypted e-mail to the Swedish Police Authority on 5 February 2019, a second time after a similar mistake. It also stored 108 such protocols in the cloud service Box without adequate security measures, and did not report the e-mail incident to the authority or document it. The Datainspektionen found infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR and of Articles 33(1) and 33(5) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 550,000 in total.

The Hungarian authority opened an ex officio investigation into how the Budapest University of Technology and Economics handled applications for regular social scholarships, after an anonymous report. The university demanded a very wide range of documents, including special-category data of people living in the applicant's household, going beyond what the law allowed. The authority found it had no valid legal basis for much of this data, breached purpose limitation and data minimisation, and gave inadequate information to applicants. It ordered the university to revise its data practices and information notices, delete the unlawfully processed data, and pay a fine of HUF 8,000,000.

A third party used social engineering to pose as Booking staff and gained access to hotel reservation data held by accommodations in the UAE, compromising personal data including credit card details. Booking learned of the incident on 10 January 2019 but notified the AP only on 7 February 2019, 22 days late. The AP found a violation of Article 33(1) GDPR for failing to notify within 72 hours. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 475,000, set from a base fine of EUR 525,000 reduced by EUR 50,000 for Booking's mitigating measures. The draft decision was approved through the Article 60 cooperation procedure without objections.
The Dutch DPA fined a Canada-based controller €525,000 for not appointing an EU representative despite offering services to individuals within the EU.

The Irish DPC ran an own-volition inquiry into how Twitter International Company (TIC) notified a personal data breach to it in January 2019, a breach that affected 88,726 EU/EEA data subjects. The Commissioner found that TIC infringed Article 33(1), on notifying the breach in time, and Article 33(5), because its documentation did not allow verification of compliance. A reprimand and an administrative fine were imposed. The draft decision had proposed a fine of $150,000 to $300,000. After the EDPB's binding Article 65 decision directed a higher fine, the DPC fixed it at $500,000, which it estimates at EUR 450,000.

The Hungarian DPA (NAIH) fined a travel agency €55,000 for not implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures, leading to the exposure of the personal data of its customers on a website and a search engine.

The President of the Polish Office for Personal Data Protection (UODO) imposed a fine of PLN 85,588 on an insurance company for failing to notify a personal data breach to the DPA without undue delay and for failing to notify a personal data breach without undue delay to data subjects.
The Polish DPA (UODO) imposed a fine of €3000 on a company for failing to respond to DPA's letters and provide access to personal data and other information necessary to carry out the DPA's tasks.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued an opinion on justification of sharing medical records with the insurance company on the basis of a cooperation agreement in the field of specialist medical examinations.

The French DPA (CNIL) imposed a fine of €20,000 on the catering company Nestor. The company sent commercial emails without gathering consent (Article L. 34-5 Postal and Electronic Communication law), it did not provide sufficient information to data subjects (Articles 12 and 13 GDPR), it failed to respect data subjects' right of access (Article 15) and finally, it did not afford sufficient security to personal data it processed (Article 32).

The Commissioner examined the Electricity Authority of Cyprus's use of the Bradford Factor to score and monitor employees' sick leave, which was applied to a staff file and fed into personal interviews and possible sanctions. The Commissioner found that this scoring had no legal basis under Article 6(1) and no Article 9(2) exception applied, so it was unlawful. The decision imposed a fine of EUR 40,000 on the Authority as controller.

Following an online inspection on 16 March 2020, the CNIL found that cookies were automatically placed on the terminals of users in France visiting the search engine page, without prior information or consent, and that the opt-out mechanism was partly defective. The CNIL rejected the argument that the Irish authority should be lead authority under the one-stop-shop, treating the matter as falling under the ePrivacy rules transposed in Article 82 of the French law. It fined Google LLC EUR 60 million and Google Ireland Limited EUR 40 million for breach of Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act. It also ordered both to inform users clearly of cookie purposes and how to refuse them, with a penalty of EUR 100,000 per day of delay after three months, and ordered the decision to be published, naming the companies for two years.

The CNIL's restricted committee fined a Luxembourg company that runs a French e-commerce site EUR 35 million. Following online checks in late 2019 and 2020, the CNIL found that cookies were placed on users' terminals in France before they gave consent and without adequate information, which breaches Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (the national transposition of ePrivacy Article 5(3)). The company argued that only the Luxembourg authority was competent, and the CNIL rejected this. The CNIL also ordered compliance within three months under a EUR 100,000 per day penalty and ordered publication of the decision.

A Paris doctor opened the ports of his home internet box and enabled the server function of imaging software, leaving more than 5,300 series of patients' medical images freely accessible for about four months. The data was also not encrypted on his computers. After a press report, the CNIL ran an online inspection and found the exposure. The restricted committee found breaches of Article 32 (security) and Article 33 (no breach notification to the CNIL) and imposed a fine of EUR 3,000, to be published without naming him. The Conseil d'Etat later reduced the fine to EUR 2,500 because there was no obligation to notify the CNIL of a breach it already knew about.
The French DPA (CNIL) imposed a fine of €7300 on the company PERFOMECLIC for sending commercial prospecting emails without proof of prior consent and without providing satisfactory information.

Datatilsynet fined Gveik AS NOK 75,000 for running a credit check on an individual with no customer relationship or other connection to the company, which had no legal basis under Article 6 GDPR and breached the accountability principle in Article 5(2). The check was run by a company representative who meant to cancel it but it went through anyway; the company admitted it should not have been run. Datatilsynet also ordered Gveik AS to set up internal control and written routines for credit checks, with confirmation due by 11 January 2021.

The Norwegian DPA fined a company NOK 400,000 (about €37,600) for enabling automatic forwarding of an employee's emails during a sick leave, without informing the employee or accepting her objection. The company appealed the fine and although the Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernnemnda) agreed with the DPA that the fine was correct, it reduced it to NOK 250,000 only because of the DPA's long case processing time.

The DPA issued an opinion on making the council meetings open to public. The DPA suggested to determine the rules regarding the openness of meetings and in the case of dealing with personal data, close the specific meeting (partially) to the public, or provide an appropriate legal basis.

The DPA issued an opinion on video surveillance in an apartment building with three separate entrances. It is necessary to obtain consent from all the co-owners of the building, unless they regulated their mutual relations in such a way that the parts with separate entrances represent independent condominium property.

The Polish DPA fined Virgin Mobile PLN 1,968,524 (the decision gives EUR 460,000 at the National Bank of Poland’s rate of 28 January 2020, 1 EUR = PLN 4.2794) for lack of appropriate technical and organisational measures, which resulted in a data breach affecting over 114,000 persons.

The Swedish DPA, Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten, did not fine a healthcare provider for breaches that in most cases result in fines. The DPA considered it disproportionate as the healthcare provider proactively tried to comply with the rules.

The Swedish DPA examined how Aleris Sjukvård AB, a health care provider, managed access to its TakeCare patient record system. It found that Aleris had not carried out a needs and risk analysis before granting access rights, and had not limited users' access to what they needed for their work, in breach of Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR. It imposed a single combined administrative fine of SEK 15,000,000 and ordered Aleris to carry out and document a needs and risk analysis and assign individual, need-limited access rights.

The Swedish DPA inspected the health care provider Aleris Närsjukvård AB in April 2019. It found that the company had not carried out a needs and risk analysis before assigning access rights in its TakeCare and NPÖ patient record systems, and that it did not limit users' access to what they need for their work. The DPA imposed a joint administrative fine of SEK 12,000,000 for breaches of Articles 5(1)(f) and 5(2) and Articles 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR. It also ordered the company to carry out and document the analysis and assign individual, limited access rights.

The Swedish Data Protection Authority inspected Region Östergötland's use of the Cosmic patient record system in April 2019. It found that the region had not carried out a documented needs and risk analysis before granting users access, and that user permissions were not limited to what each person needs for their work. The authority imposed a combined administrative fine of SEK 2,500,000 for breaches of the principles and security rules, and ordered the region to carry out and document a needs and risk analysis and to assign access rights accordingly.

The Swedish supervisory authority inspected how the health and medical care committee of Region Västerbotten managed access to the NCS Cross patient record system. It found that the committee had not carried out a needs and risk analysis before granting user access rights, and had not limited users' access to what their work required. The authority found infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR and imposed a joint administrative fine of SEK 2,500,000. It also ordered the committee to carry out and document the required needs and risk analysis and then assign individual access rights.

The Swedish Data Protection Authority inspected Sahlgrenska University Hospital in April 2019 and found that it had not carried out a needs and risk analysis before granting staff access to its Melior and NPÖ patient record systems, and that user access was not limited to what each person needs for their work. The logs in Melior also did not show which actions were taken on patient data. The authority found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR and imposed one joint administrative fine of SEK 3,500,000, which it treated as connected processing under Article 83(3). It also ordered the hospital to carry out and document the analysis, set individual access rights and fix the logs; it did not fine the logging deficiency separately.

The Swedish DPA inspected Karolinska University Hospital's TakeCare patient record system in March 2019. It found that the hospital had granted staff access without first carrying out a needs and risk analysis, and that the access rights given were too broad, so that users could reach almost all patient records. It imposed a combined administrative fine of SEK 4,000,000 under Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR. It also ordered the hospital to carry out and document the analysis and to assign individual access rights limited to what each user needs.

The Swedish DPA supervised Capio S:t Görans Sjukhus AB, an emergency hospital in Stockholm, on how it assigned access rights to patient records in the Cosmic, NPÖ and TakeCare systems. It found that the hospital had not carried out needs-and-risk analyses before assigning access, and had not limited users' access to what their work required. The DPA found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR. It imposed a single joint administrative fine of SEK 30,000,000 and ordered the hospital to carry out and document needs-and-risk analyses and then assign individual, limited access.

The Czech Office for Personal Data Protection issued a penalty order (příkaz) against company I., which runs an online auction portal. The company did not answer the complainant's requests of 31 March and 2 July 2020 to delete a public auction notice containing his name, date of birth and address, and it did not act after the Office's warning of 29 July 2020. The Office found a breach of the right to erasure under Article 17(1)(a) GDPR and of the duty to inform about measures under Article 12(3) GDPR, and imposed a fine of CZK 50,000. Only one data subject was affected, and the fine was set at the lower end of the penalty range.

The Czech Office issued a penalty order (příkaz) against a company that kept sending marketing SMS messages to a former employee's phone after he had repeatedly objected to direct marketing in September and October 2019. The Office had warned the company in June 2020, and the company said it then stopped processing the data for marketing. A further marketing SMS was sent on 2 October 2020, which the Office treated as a breach of the right to erasure under Article 17(1)(c) GDPR. The company was fined 30,000 CZK.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a reduced fine of €1200 on the defendant for illicit use of personal data in violation of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.

Icelandic DPA held that the treatment of an e-mail box by a company at the time of complainant's termination of employment did not comply with the provisions of the Icelandic Act on Data Protection and the Processing of Personal Data.

This is the DVI Director's decision on an internal appeal by the online retailer HH Invest against the DVI official's decision of 8 October 2020. That decision fined the company EUR 15,000 and ordered it to bring its processing on xnet.lv into line with the GDPR. The DVI found that the privacy information was not transparent, that customers were not given a clear initial chance to object to marketing emails sent to addresses obtained in a purchase, and that analytics cookies were used without consent or an easy way to refuse or withdraw it. The Director rejected all of the company's arguments, including those about the lack of harm, the lack of complaints, procedural deadlines and the reasoning for the fine. The Director rejected the appeal and left the fine and the orders unchanged. The company can challenge the decision in the district court.

A doctor complained about a report on the TV programme 'Le Iene' in which journalists entered his medical practice without identifying themselves, pretending to be unwell, and filmed him with hidden cameras. His face was only partly blurred and he stayed recognisable by voice, clothing and workplace. The Garante found that the hidden-camera method was not shown to be necessary, as the information could have been obtained by other means, and that the anonymisation measures were inadequate. It found breaches of the fairness and lawfulness principle, upheld the complaint, banned further processing of the complainant's data except for storage, fined the broadcaster EUR 10,000 and ordered publication. No action was taken on the access request (Art. 15).

A trade union reported that a call-centre company had adopted a 'locker policy' requiring employees to keep medicines, medical devices and sanitary products visible on their desks. The Garante found that this exposed employees' health-related information to colleagues and superiors without any valid legal basis, and breached the lawfulness and data minimisation principles. The policy applied from 20 June to 24 July 2019. The Garante ordered the company to bring its new locker policy into line with the GDPR and fined it EUR 20,000.

A complaint was lodged about video surveillance at a hotel, which was allegedly also used to monitor staff. An inspection by the Garante's special privacy unit in October 2019 found 17 cameras, no information signs, and a system set up to display images without recording. The Garante found that the hotel had failed to provide the required information to people under surveillance (Art. 13 GDPR) and breached the fairness principle (Art. 5(1)(a) GDPR). It imposed a fine of EUR 3,000, ordered publication of the decision, and dropped the charge under Art. 88 GDPR and Art. 114 of the Italian Code, finding no evidence of staff monitoring.

A man complained that a health inspector from the Southern Health Inspection Authority visited his home, photographed his property and movable goods, and was not given enough information, and he asked for the data to be deleted. Persónuvernd found that the authority could rely on the public-interest and legal-obligation grounds for the registration and photographing, that the basic principles were met, and that the processing complied with the GDPR and the Icelandic Data Protection Act. The deletion request was not granted because records must be kept under Icelandic archive law, and disposal is for the National Archives to decide.

The Romanian authority closed an investigation into DADA CREATION S.R.L. after a report that a document with detailed order records of its website customers, including minors' data, was publicly accessible. It found the company had not applied adequate technical and organisational security measures, leading to unauthorised disclosure of the data of about 1091 individuals. It fined the company RON 24,272.50 (about EUR 5,000) under Article 32 and issued a warning for failing to notify the breach under Article 33. It also ordered the company to review and update its security measures.

The Social Committee of Gnosjö Municipality ran real-time camera surveillance of a resident in their bedroom in a LSS housing facility from March 2019 to April 2020, to protect the resident from serious self-harm. The Authority found no legal basis for the monitoring, found it disproportionate and not transparent, and found that the resident was not informed and that no impact assessment or prior consultation had been carried out. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 200,000 for infringements of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1), 9(2), 13, 35 and 36 and of the national camera surveillance law, section 15.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) imposed a fine of € 1500 on a private individual for the unlawful filming of public roads and private property of third parties with surveillance cameras, and for illegally sharing images taken from this system in breach of Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. There were legitimate interests for the defendants to install surveillance cameras to protect their own private property. But the way those surveillance cameras were positioned and the fact that they were constantly monitoring was not deemed necessary to safeguard those legitimate interests. The DPA moreover found the interests of the defendants to process personal data through the surveillance cameras to be overridden by the interests of the complainants and other data subjects. On the contrary, the taking of a one-off photograph with a smartphone, as a direct response to seeing an alleged offence, was seen as constituting a lawful processing within the meaning of Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR.

A skier complained that the ski lift operator took a reference photo at the lift gates and compared it with a check photo to stop misuse of lift passes, and that he could not avoid this when buying a pass. The authority held that the operator could rely on legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, since the photo comparison serves access control, is limited in scope and storage, and was expected by the skier. A plain photo used only for visual comparison is not biometric data under Article 9(1) GDPR. The complaint was dismissed as unfounded, and the decision is final.

The Swedish DPA investigated the School Platform used by the City of Stockholm after receiving personal data breach notifications from the Education Committee. It found security failings in four subsystems: access rights that were too broad, guardians who could reach other pupils' records, and an administration interface reachable through search engines that exposed staff with protected identity. The Committee was found to have breached Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1) and 35. The authority fined it SEK 4,000,000 for the Article 5 and 32 breaches and ordered it to carry out proper impact assessments and restrict access rights in the school-attendance module.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) sanctioned the company RECAMBIOS VILLALEGRE S.L. with a fine of €12000 for publishing images of a person on social networks without a legal basis and for the lack of informative posters on the installed video surveillance system.

The Swedish DPA investigated the Education Board of the City of Stockholm after a series of personal data breach notifications about unauthorised access to pupil data in the city's school platform. It found insufficient technical and organisational security in several subsystems, including over-broad access rights in the school attendance module, and failure to carry out data protection impact assessments. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 4,000,000 and ordered the board to restrict access rights and carry out impact assessments.

The Romanian DPA press release (published 22.12.2020) says it completed an investigation at C&V Water Control S.A. on 20.11.2020. The company had not supplied the information the authority requested, in breach of the GDPR provisions on the authority's investigative powers. It was fined 9746 lei (about EUR 2000) as a contravention sanction and ordered to send the authority all information requested in earlier letters.

The Hessian DPA (HBDI) held that a controller may not require a signature as identification for access requests pursuant to Article 12(6) GDPR, and has to respond to access requests via other transport mediums than postal mail.

The Austrian DPA held that a Viennese restaurant was not allowed to collect data of a customer for contact tracing regarding COVID-19 infections: consent under Article 9(2)(a) GDPR could not be considered as freely given in this context and the Viennese Regulation on Contact Tracing did not contain a sufficient legal obligation under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR and Article 9(2)(i) GDPR.

A company took personal data of industrial property owners from public registers and sent them unsolicited commercial offers without any legal basis. One owner objected and asked for erasure on 8 September 2020, and the company never informed him of any action taken. The Office found two misdemeanours (Art. 6(1) and Art. 12(3) GDPR) and, applying the absorption principle, imposed a single fine of CZK 120,000 plus CZK 1,000 costs. The company had not responded in the proceedings. The earlier penalty order of CZK 150,000 was cancelled after the company objected.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined Vodafone for concluding a contract made fraudulently in the complainant's name. This was in breach of Article 6(1) GDPR (lawfulness of processing). Vodafone payed the reduced fine of €36000 (guilty, voluntary and early payment).

After ZOO, the Copenhagen Zoo, notified a personal data breach on 3 January 2020, the Danish DPA found that a login page for annual pass holders could be brute-forced easily (four-digit passwords, no lockout), exposing names, addresses, emails and card numbers. The DPA issued a severe reprimand for breaches of Articles 32, 33, 34 and 5(1)(a), and ordered ZOO to notify all affected data subjects at high risk and to correct the earlier misleading information. No fine was imposed in this decision.

The French DPA (CNIL) fined Carrefour Banque € 800000 for several violations of the GDPR and French data protection law. The breaches concerned loyalty and transparency of data processing, accessibility and content of information concerning processing and illicit use of cookies.

The French DPA (CNIL) imposed a € 2250000 fine on Carrefour France for several violations of the GDPR and French data protection law. These include: excessive data retention periods, incomplete and unclear information on data processes, lack of proper answer to data subjects' requests, security breaches and illicit use of cookies.
The Hungarian DPA (NAIH) issued a fine of €28 on a controller for failing to meet an administrative deadline to rectify the data subject's outdated email address.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a warning sanction against the Secretary General for Innovation and Quality of the Public Justice Service for a security breach (Articles 5(1)(f), 25, 32 and 34 GDPR), in the process of granting nationality and residence to immigrants.

The Norwegian DPA (Datatilsynet) fined Indre Østfold municipality €18,860 for publishing a former student's school folder openly on their website, therefore breaching Articles 32(1)(b), (5), and (6) of the GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) terminated a sanctioning procedure against VODAFONE ESPAÑA S.A.U. for infringing Article 6(1) GDPR. Vodafone, recognising its responsibility, made an early payment of €42000 (reduced from the original €70000 fine).

After a complaint from a visitor, the Danish DPA examined the cookie consent banner on the golf.dk website operated by DGU Erhverv A/S. The banner offered no way to refuse processing, bundled several purposes including statistics and marketing, and treated continued use of the site as consent. The DPA found that the consent was not freely given, not granular and not an unambiguous indication of wishes, and issued a reprimand for breach of Article 6(1)(a) GDPR. No fine was imposed.

Ticketmaster UK Limited suffered a personal data breach in 2018, in which customer data was compromised through a chat bot on its website, affecting about 9.4 million EEA data subjects. The Commissioner found that Ticketmaster failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data, infringing Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR. A penalty notice under section 155 DPA 2018 was issued, imposing a fine of GBP 1,250,000, reduced from a proposed GBP 1,500,000 after Ticketmaster's representations on the financial impact of COVID-19.

A candidate tenant lodged six complaints against a Flemish social housing company over website security and cookies, privacy notices, access rights, the processing of medical data, smart meter readings and camera surveillance. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of the lawfulness and transparency principles, including Article 6 and Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. It ordered the company to bring its processing into compliance within three months and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 1,500. The Chamber held that a private-law social housing company does not fall within the public-authority exemption in Article 83(7) GDPR.

The Garante investigated Vodafone Italia after hundreds of complaints and reports about unsolicited telemarketing calls and messages made by or for the company. It found that Vodafone lacked controls over the chain of personal data collection, used contact lists from third parties without valid consent, ignored objections to marketing, had inadequate security of its customer databases, failed to notify a data breach, and did not fully act on data subject requests. The Garante ordered Vodafone to respond to the complainants, adapt its telemarketing and database security, and banned further marketing using third-party lists without valid consent. It imposed a fine of EUR 12,251,601 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Polish DPA (UODO) issued a reprimand on a waste management company and ordered it to notify data subjects of a breach. The unauthorised disclosure involved a list containing addresses of persons subject to medical quarantine.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) held that a municipal council (Ayuntamiento de Mejorada del Campo) was in violation of Article 37(1)(a) GDPR as it did not designate a data protection officer despite being a public authority which processes personal data.

The Irish DPA (DPC) found that Ryanair infringed Article 15 of the GDPR by failing to provide the complainant with a copy their personal data. The DPC was acting in its capacity as lead supervisory authority, to examine the complaint originally received by the UK Data Protection Authority.

The Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernrådet) unanimously overturned the Norwegian DPA’s (Datatilsynet) decision and held that a name which contained an incorrect uppercase letter did not constitute incorrect personal data which needs to be rectified based on Article 16.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of € 8000 on Asociación de Víctimas por Arbitrariedades Judiciales (JAVA). JAVA infringed Article 6(1)(a) GDPR by publishing illegal recordings on its website and also infringed Article 22(2) LSSI due to its cookie policy.

A hospital was retaining a part of the salary of its employees being members of a trade union. This practice was based on an oral agreement with the work council, plus a written document from the employees. However, the DPA concluded that - the consent could not be considered as valid due to the fact that no mention made of the right of the employees to withdraw their consent. The litigation chamber also concluded that the precise purpose was not expressly communicated to the data subjects. No sanction was issued, considering that the processing at stake was stopped in June 2019.

The Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernrådet) overturned the Norwegian DPA's (Datatilsynet) decision to ban Arendal municipality from using a digital form to survey bullying behaviour at their local schools.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a penalty of € 20000 on XFERA MOVILES S.A. for failing to comply with its obligation to cooperate with the supervisory authority under Article 31 GDPR in conjunction with Article 58(1)(e) GDPR.

A complainant argued that the Public Employment Service Austria disclosed his social insurance number to his bank when transferring an unemployment benefit payment, and that this number is health data under Article 9 GDPR. The DSB held that the social insurance number was used only as an identifier and not as health data, and that the processing was lawful and proportionate. The complaint was dismissed as unfounded.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation on 4 November 2020 into Vodafone România and found breaches of Articles 12, 15 and 17 GDPR. Complaints alleged Vodafone had not answered requests for access and erasure. Vodafone could not prove it had handled the requests within the Article 12 time limit. It was fined 19,468.8 lei (about EUR 4,000) and ordered to send the complainant a reply on the measures taken.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €1500 on Raise Marketing SL for a marketing call where the recipient was included on the "Robinson List". This was in violation of Articles 21 GDPR and 23 Spanish data protection law (LOPDGDD).

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) held that Vodafone infringed Article 6(1) GDPR by sending the complainant an SMS asking for the payment of a fraudulent contractual service. Vodafone was fined €30000 (guilty, voluntary and early payment reduction applied).
The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) sanctioned the defendant for publishing videos in which the neighbour's house and the neighbour's contact details are clearly visible in violation of Article 6(1) GDPR.

The Information Commissioner’s Officer (ICO) imposed a fine of € 20.7 million on Marriott International Inc (“Marriott”) for failing to ensure appropriate security when processing its costumers’ personal data, thus violating Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR. Investigations began following notification of an attack on Marriott’s IT systems that took place over a period of time that includes May 2018 (when the GDPR came into force) to September 2018 . As a result, the attacker(s) had access to vast amounts of costumers’ personal data: Marriot estimated that they accessed 339 million guest records, with 30.1 million being EEA members’ records and 7 million being associated with the UK.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a warning to Escuela Infantil (nursery school) for the infringement of Article 13 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) has imposed three different warning sanctions on the Department of Education of the Government of Navarra for infringing Articles 5(1)(a), 9(1), and 13 GDPR on the processing of data from surveys answered by schoolchildren.

A former employee complained that his individual company email account stayed active after he left in March 2018 and that the company accessed and kept its contents, despite telling him it would be deleted after 60 days. The company's IT administrator went into the mailbox in June 2018, extracted 75 emails and used 32 of them in court proceedings against the ex-employee. The Garante found the processing unlawful, with no adequate information given to the employee and the company's email rules breaching data protection principles. It banned further use of the extracted data (except for legal defence) and of employee mailbox data kept under the company rules, ordered the company to bring its May 2020 email policy into line with the GDPR, and fined it EUR 20,000.

Three people who had worked at the company's premises under a catering contract complained about its video surveillance system. An inspection found no information notices, two cameras installed in 2017 beyond those authorised by the labour inspectorate, and remote access to the footage that the authorisation had said would not exist. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), 13 and 88 GDPR and Article 114 of the Italian Code. It fined the company EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The company had meanwhile complied.

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) held that a controller breached the GDPR by not conducting a legitimate interest assessment and by not substantiating how its interest outweighed those of the data subject in the context of direct marketing communications.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €5000 on a betting company because its installation of cameras did not comply with Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a penalty of € 4000 on ORGANIC NATUR 03 S.L. for the infringement of Article 13 GDPR (data privacy policy) and a warning penalty for the infringement of Article 7 GDPR regarding the collection of customer consent.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €50000 on Conseguridad SL for not having a data protection officer in violation of Article 37(1)(b) GDPR in conjunction with Articles 34(1)(ñ) and 34(3) LOPDGDD.
An individual lodged a complaint with the Spanish DPA (AEPD) for considering the processing of his personal data by a law firm contrary to data protection regulations (Article 6 GDPR).

The Hungarian authority opened an ex officio investigation into a shoe retailer after a customer asked to see and have preserved CCTV footage of a disputed purchase and was refused. The company had no internal rules on CCTV data subject requests when the GDPR became applicable, and its later policy of 26 November 2019 still disproportionately restricted access and restriction rights. The authority found violations of Articles 12(4), 15(1), 18(1)(c) and 25(1) and imposed a fine of HUF 20,000,000.

The Norwegian DPA fined Østfold Hospital €64,400 (NOK 750,000) for insufficiently protecting patient data cf. Article 32 GDPR and Article 5(1)(f) GDPR and inadequate internal controls cf. Article 24 GDPR and Article 5(2) GDPR.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) held that posting the name and outstanding debt of the claimant on a public notice board was in violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.
Lithuanian DPA imposes a fine of EUR 15.000,00 for a failure to implement sufficient technical and organizational measures with regards to education procedures of an adopted child.

The Romanian supervisory authority finished an investigation on 15 September 2020 into the company Globus Score SRL. It found that the company had not carried out the corrective measure ordering it to provide the information the authority had requested. The company was fined RON 9,713.14, stated as equivalent to EUR 2,000, and was again ordered to send the authority all the requested information.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) held that a bank had the right to request from an individual more detailed information about their assets, if the individual had been flagged as a "politically exposed person" under the national anti-money laundering legislation. The bank's position was held to be in accordance with Article 6(1)(c) GDPR.

The Cyprus DPA held that the inability of the data controller to discover the original contract with the data subject constitutes a violation of the right to access the personal data. A fine of € 15000 was issued.

The Austrian DSB issued a penal order (Strafverfügung) against a private individual who, from February to June 2020, published excerpts of patients' letters, medical findings and other medical records on his personal Facebook page. The published data included patient names, diagnoses, medication data, hospital admission and discharge dates and social insurance numbers. The DSB found a breach of the principle of lawfulness (Art. 5(1)(a)) and of the ban on processing health data without a valid exception (Art. 9(1) and (2)) and imposed a fine of EUR 600. The penal order is final.
The Austrian DPA imposed a fine of €150 on a person for secretly filming a woman with his smartphone while she was using a public restroom.
The Hungarian DPA (NAIH) issued a warning to MarkMyProfessor Media Advertising for failing to provide transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of data subject rights.

The Spanish DPA fined an airline €30,000 for not allowing their website's users to exercise a choice regarding cookies before placing them, as well as for not offering enough information about cookies and not allowing users to reject all cookies at once.
The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) fined British Airways €22 million for failing to protect the personal and financial details of more than 400,000 of its customers.

The Romanian supervisory authority completed an investigation into S.C. Marsorom S.R.L. on 21.09.2020, following a complaint that some customers' personal data could be viewed on the company's website. It found that the company had not adopted sufficient security measures to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure, breaching Articles 25 and 32 GDPR. The company was fined 14574.9 RON, stated as the equivalent of EUR 3000. The authority also recommended a shorter storage period for customer account data under Article 5(1)(e).

A man complained that the municipality of Collegno gave a traffic-fine notice with a non-compliant privacy notice, lacked signage, and never answered his access request sent by certified email on 12 March 2019. The Garante found the information and signage complaints unfounded and closed them. It found the municipality answered the access request only on 13 February 2020, far beyond one month, did not tell him the reasons or his remedies, and had no appropriate internal procedure until 15 January 2020. It fined the municipality EUR 2,000 under Article 12(1), (3) and (4) GDPR and ordered publication of the decision.

An employee complained that a staff welfare union, ΤΕΥ-ΑΤΗΚ, had handled her personal data in a way she could not get access to, and the Commissioner examined how the employer's database was shared with the union. The union's staff could view photos and contact and job details of employees who were not union members, through the employer's intranet. The employer removed that access for non-members on 31 March 2020 and cut the union staff with access from nine to one. The Commissioner decided not to impose a fine at this stage, but ordered the employer to adopt measures so the union has no access disproportionate to its purpose, excluding member photos, and to report back within two months.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company running a website that holds personal data of people, some registered without their knowledge. The company sent e-mails to people who had not registered and to a person who repeatedly asked for erasure, ignored erasure requests made after objections, and demanded a 500 CZK fee to process erasure requests. The authority found breaches of Articles 6(1), 12(3) and 12(5) GDPR. Under the absorption principle it imposed one fine of CZK 300,000, based on the most serious offence.

A warehouse employee complained that the employer's security camera system also monitored workers, including a room used for short administrative work, and that staff were not properly told about the cameras. The authority upheld the complaint. It found that the camera angle in one room breached purpose limitation and data minimisation, and that employees were not adequately informed between 18 November 2019 and 3 April 2020. It ordered the camera's angle to be changed, imposed a fine of HUF 700,000 and ordered publication of the decision without identifying data. The authority also awarded the applicant HUF 10,000 because it exceeded the procedural deadline.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) argued that the installation of security cameras must always be done in accordance with Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, concerning the minimisation of data processed.

The UK DPA (ICO) served an Enforcement Notice against the credit reference agency Experian, after it found that Experian violated the transparency principle and failed to uphold data subject rights. Experian must make significant changes to how it handles people’s personal data in its direct marketing practices – or face sanctions.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined Lycamobile S.L. €60000 for processing personal data without the consent of the respective data subject, therefore infringing Article 6(1)(a) GDPR.

Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) issued a €44000 fine against Studios MG Limited for sending unsolicited marketing emails advertising protective face masks, in breach of the Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003 (PECR).

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) considered that it was not competent to rule in a binding manner as to whether processing of personal data by a media entity for journalistic purposes breached the Icelandic Act 90/2018 or the GDPR. Instead, it considered that a court should balance the right to freedom of expression and the right to privacy.

The Hamburg data protection authority fined H&M's Hamburg-based company about EUR 35.3 million for monitoring several hundred employees at the Nuremberg service centre. Since at least 2014, managers had recorded details of employees' private lives, including illnesses, diagnoses, family problems and religious beliefs, after 'Welcome Back Talks' and informal conversations. The notes were stored on a network drive, at times readable by up to 50 other managers, and used to profile staff. The authority learned of it through press reports, froze and obtained the data, and questioned witnesses. The company then apologised, agreed to pay staff compensation and presented a new data protection concept; the authority welcomed the compensation.

The Romanian authority fined Megareduceri TV S.R.L. 14,519.1 lei (stated as the equivalent of EUR 3,000) for not complying with a corrective measure, namely failing to answer the authority's requests. The investigation started after several complainants reported receiving marketing SMS messages on their personal phones without having given consent. The company was also ordered to send the authority its answers to the earlier requests within 5 calendar days.

The press release of 1 October 2020 reports two sanctions; the second concerns a homeowners' association in Chiajna, Ilfov. A complainant said the association had not answered his request, and the association then failed to carry out the corrective measure requiring it to answer the authority's requests. The authority fined it RON 9,659 (stated as equivalent to EUR 2,000) and ordered it to send the requested information in writing within 5 calendar days. The first sanction in the release, against a different company, is not part of this decision.
